record.original_question: Find the smallest integer k > 1 for which there exists an integer n such that gcd(n, n + k) = 1 while gcd(n + i, n + k) > 1 for every integer i with 1 ≤ i < k.

evidence.quote: Find the smallest integer k > 1 and an integer n such that gcd(n, n + k) = 1 and gcd(n + i, n + k) > 1 for each i, 1 ≤ i < k.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Determine the smallest integer k > 1 for which there exists a positive integer n such that gcd(n, n + k) = 1 and, for every integer i with 1 ≤ i < k, gcd(n + i, n(n + k)) > 1 (equivalently, every integer strictly between n and n + k shares a prime factor with n or with n + k). Exhibit such an n for the optimal k.
artifact.status_search_result: This is the classical Pillai problem on consecutive integers. Pillai and Brauer proved that the smallest such k equals 17; for every k ≥ 17 such an n exists, and for 1 < k ≤ 16 no such n exists. The problem is considered solved.

status_evidence.title: Pillai's Problem on Consecutive Integers
status_evidence.snippet: Pillai's problem on m consecutive integers and gcd conditions; results due to Pillai and Brauer.
status_evidence.claim: The threshold value 17 was established by Pillai and Brauer for the consecutive-integer gcd problem.

status_evidence.title: Pillai's Problem on Consecutive Integers (preprint)
status_evidence.snippet: For sequences of integers, the threshold is 17, by results of Pillai and Brauer.
status_evidence.claim: The smallest k for which the desired n exists is 17.
